prompt: The robot ahead of you turns green. What does this allow you to do?
options: Proceed immediately — a green light guarantees you the right of way
Scan the intersection and proceed only once the way is clear
You must proceed; stopping while the light is green is not permitted
explanation: Green is permission to go only when the way ahead is actually clear, so you still scan the intersection before moving. It does not guarantee that cross traffic has stopped, and it never forces you to move into a situation that is unsafe.
note: RR7 object carries no citation — attach the traffic-signal regulation before approval.

prompt: You are approaching a robot at speed and the light changes to amber when you are only about a car's length from the stop line. Stopping would need violent braking, and there is a vehicle close behind you. What should you do?
options: Brake as hard as you can and stop before the line
Accelerate to clear the intersection before the light turns red
Continue through at your current speed, because you cannot stop safely
explanation: Amber means stop if you can do so safely — at that distance you cannot, so you carry on through at the speed you are already doing. Emergency braking invites the car behind into your boot, and speeding up to beat the light is exactly the fault the examiner is watching for.

prompt: Your light is green, but traffic on the far side of the intersection is backed up and there is no space for your car to come out the other side. What should you do?
options: Enter the intersection and wait there — the green light gives you the right to be in it
Wait behind the stop line until there is room for you on the far side
Enter as long as you can stop with your rear bumper clear of the stop line
explanation: Green only lets you go when the way is clear, and it is not clear if you would come to a standstill inside the intersection and block the cross traffic. Neither the green light nor keeping your bumper past the line gives you permission to obstruct the intersection.

prompt: The robot ahead turns red as you approach. Where must your vehicle come to a stop?
options: Behind the stop line
With your front wheels resting on the stop line so you can still see the light
Far enough forward to be level with the traffic light itself
explanation: Red means stop behind the line — the space in front of it belongs to pedestrians and crossing traffic. Creeping onto the line or up to the signal head puts your car where other road users need to be, and counts as crossing the line on red.

prompt: The light turns amber while you are still several car lengths back. You could stop before the line, but it would take firm braking. Nothing is following you closely. What does the rule require?
options: Carry on through — you are too close to stop comfortably
Brake firmly but under control and stop behind the line
Carry on through, because braking firmly on amber is never safe
explanation: Amber asks whether you can stop safely, not whether it would be comfortable — with a clear road behind you, controlled firm braking is safe, so you stop. Only when a safe stop is genuinely impossible may you continue through.

prompt: You need to pull over for a moment to drop a friend off in a busy street. Which of these places may you legally stop?
options: Right on the pedestrian crossing, with your hazard lights on
In a marked bay in the side street, well clear of the corner
Just around the corner of the intersection, with two wheels on the pavement
explanation: A marked bay clear of the corner is the only choice that neither blocks traffic nor sits on or near a crossing or intersection. Hazard lights do not make an illegal stop legal, and stopping right at an intersection hides you and your passengers from approaching drivers.
note: RR9 object carries no citation; attach NRTR 2000 stopping/parking regs before approval.

prompt: In good, dry conditions you keep a two-second gap to the vehicle in front. What should that gap become in heavy rain?
options: Four seconds or more
Still two seconds — the gap does not change with the weather
One second, so you stay close enough to see the vehicle's brake lights
explanation: On a wet road it takes you much longer to pull up, so the two-second gap is stretched to four seconds or more. Keeping the same gap ignores the longer stopping distance, and closing up to one second leaves you no room at all to react.
note: Two-to-four-second guidance is defensive-driving practice, not a numeric legal limit — flag at review.

prompt: Thick fog rolls in and visibility drops sharply. Apart from slowing down, what should you do?
options: Put your hazard lights on and keep your normal speed
Switch your headlights on and lengthen your following distance
Tuck in close behind the vehicle ahead and follow its tail lights
explanation: Headlights make you visible to others and a longer gap buys you time when you can only see a short way ahead. Hazard lights at normal speed still leave you arriving too fast to stop, and following someone's tail lights closely means you inherit their crash.

prompt: You are on a road signposted 100 km/h. It is raining steadily and the light is fading. May you drive at 100 km/h?
options: Yes — the sign sets the speed you are expected to drive
Yes, as long as your headlights are on
No — the sign is a maximum for good conditions, so drop your speed to suit the wet road and poor light
explanation: A speed limit is a ceiling for good conditions, not a target, and rain plus poor light means you need to be slower than the sign allows. Treating the number as the expected speed, or thinking headlights cancel out the loss of grip, is how learners lose control in the wet.

prompt: Why exactly does a wet or slippery road force you to leave a bigger following gap?
options: Your stopping distance gets longer because the tyres grip less once you brake
Your reaction time gets slower when it rains
Vehicles ahead of you brake harder in the wet
explanation: Rain changes the braking part of the equation — with less grip the car travels further after you hit the brakes, so you need more space in hand. Your reaction time is set by you, not the weather, and there is no rule that says the car ahead brakes harder in the wet.

prompt: In which of these situations may you legally be out of your seatbelt while the vehicle is moving?
options: While you are reversing or moving into or out of a parking bay
While you are driving slowly in a quiet residential street
While you are the front passenger on a very short trip
explanation: The only exception is reversing or manoeuvring in and out of a parking bay, where the belt would stop you turning to see behind you. A low speed or a short trip changes nothing — anyone in a seat fitted with a belt must be wearing it.
note: Restricted to B/C/EB — motorcycles have no seatbelts.

prompt: You are giving a five-year-old a lift and there is no child seat in your car. What must happen?
options: He must wear the seatbelt fitted to that seat
He may travel unrestrained, because no child restraint is available
He must share an adult's seatbelt on that adult's lap
explanation: A child uses a child restraint when one is available, and a seatbelt when one is not — so the belt goes on. Leaving him loose is never allowed, and two people in one belt means the adult's weight is thrown onto the child in a crash.
note: Built on the 3-14 child band, deliberately NOT the under-3 infant rule (reg 213(6A)) which is secondary-source only.
